x: Wafer filters Right-click a wafer in the Deck to choose what it accepts. A wafer with no filters accepts everything. The rows work as described in Type Filters. Void An Allow row has a Void key. With it on, anything of that kind that doesn't fit on the wafer is destroyed. Filling order Wafers fill from left to right. When several kinds arrive together, the higher Allow rows take space first. Empty out The same window has an Empty out button. It moves everything on that wafer onto the Deck's other wafers, and each item costs the usual charge. Nothing is ever destroyed this way. What finds no room stays where it is.

Type Filters Wafers, ports and bays share the same filter. It decides which items and fluids get through. Rows A filter is a list of rows. Each row has a type and a mode. Type Matches Material One item or fluid by its ID, such as Tag Everything in a tag, such as Mod ID Everything from one mod, such as Allow lets matches through, Deny keeps them out. The first enabled row that matches decides. The arrows change the order. Rows can be switched off without removing them. Item components, such as enchantments or names, are ignored. Unmatched items With at least one enabled Allow row, anything that matches no row is refused. With only Deny rows, everything else gets through. An empty filter lets everything through, except on an Output Port, which then sends nothing. Adding a row Click the slot with an item to fill in its ID. Shift-click to use what it holds instead, such as the water in a bucket. Items and fluids can also be dragged in from JEI. In Tag mode, an item with several tags shows a list to pick from.

Making chips by hand Nearly every JASM recipe is built from chips. Logic and Memory Chips need nothing but a few common blocks. Step by step Cut a Data Crystal into a Blank Chip at a Stonecutter. Cook the Blank Chip. On a Campfire it becomes an Unquenched Logic Chip ; in a Blast Furnace, an Unquenched Memory Chip. Drop the hot chip in water, still or flowing. After 2 seconds it hisses and becomes a Logic Chip or a Memory Chip. The whole stack cools at once, and no water is used up. Other chips Link Chips and Advanced chips can only be made by a Bitling in the Chip Workshop. Find out more. In bulk The Crystal Foundry makes Blank Chips straight from Crystal Seeds.

Link Chip The chip for the third tier of JASM. A Link Chip can only be made by a Bitling in the Chip Workshop. It can't be crafted by hand. What it is for Third-tier recipes need it, like the Advanced Deck, the 16K wafers and the Access Port. Hand one to a wild Bitling to make friends. A Link Bitling is made from eight of them.

Nibblings and Bytelings The grown-up stages of a Bitling. Each one works the Chip Workshop better than the last. Nibbling Makes only its own chip type, and Advanced chips more often. Battery of 200,000 FE. Needs 300 chips of training to grow up. A Link Nibbling can work a Relay Chatterbox. Byteling Makes only its own type. A switch in the Workshop picks standard or Advanced chips. Battery of 400,000 FE. The only critter that can build a Synapse Core. A Link Byteling can work a Relay Chatterbox, like a Link Nibbling. Recipes

Power Upgrade A port with a Power Upgrade passes FE from your network to the machine it faces. It is how a modded machine gets power from your network. Every port has a slot for it: Access Ports and item ports. A full block Access Port powers only the machines of the type it works with, not every block touching it. The port stores no power. Power goes straight through to the machine, as much as it takes, with no limit per tick. When there isn't enough for every machine, each machine gets an equal share. The port's screen shows how many FE a tick it is passing on. The power comes from the network: generators, Batteries or other mods through a Power Interface. Recipe

Demolition Bay Turned off on this world. Placed bays keep their contents but don't work. A Demolition Bay breaks the block in front of it into its own grid, scoops up fluids and picks up items lying in the space in front of it. Enchant it like a pickaxe for Fortune, Silk Touch and Efficiency. At a glance Speed 3 seconds, down to 0.2 seconds with 4 Speed Upgrades Breaking 6 FE for each point of cost: 1, plus the block's hardness and drops, times enchantments Scooping 50 FE a bucket Picking up 20 FE per pickup action, up to 64 items from the ground Upgrades five slots: up to four Speed Upgrades and one Redstone Upgrade Holds 10,000 FE and 16 buckets Good to know Its Input / Output key opens sides for items and fluids separately, each Output or closed. A side set to Output sends what it broke or scooped into whatever is there, and an Input Port, hopper or pipe can empty it there. Every side starts closed. It runs on cable power and doesn't take up a place on the machine limit. It also takes power from any cable or pipe, other mods' too: the Energy tab of its Input / Output key sets which sides take it. Speed Upgrades raise the power per break, scoop or pickup as well as the speed. Four upgrades cost two and a half times the power for each action. With a Redstone Upgrade it can run only while powered or unpowered, or work once for each redstone pulse. Picking up items counts as an action too. You can add filters to decide what it may or may not break. Works for items and fluids. The small speaker key next to the ? key mutes or unmutes the laser sound of every Demolition Bay, in your game only. Its opposite is the Deployment Bay. Recipe

Advanced Crafting Server A Crafting Server two blocks tall, with room for ten of everything. It runs one job at a time like the small one, but with far more Processors and Storage Modules. At a glance Slots 10 for Processors, 10 for Storage Modules Uses what its Processors use, only while it has a job. Nothing when idle Counts toward the machine limit Good to know Its front screen shows what the job makes and what is crafting right now. A key on its screen switches the front between big icons only and more details. Its parts are locked in while it works. Breaking either half breaks both, and spills whatever its job held. Servers of both kinds can share a network. A job goes to one that fits and is free. Recipe

Material Stands for one of another mod's materials, a gas for example, on a Recipe Card. It is not a real item: you can't craft it or pick it up. In a Network Encoder set to Processing, right-click a slot with a container that holds the material. The slot then shows the material and its amount. The card needs that material: the job waits until the network's storage has it. A job's list shows the material by name, like any other ingredient.

Wrench For turning machines and picking them up. Right-click a side of a JASM machine, Archive or generator to turn its front there. Sneak and right-click a JASM machine, cable or power block to pick it up at once, straight into your inventory. Anything in its slots comes too. What doesn't fit drops on the ground. It keeps what it keeps when mined. A Docking Station picks up with its Deck inside, like breaking it, and only for those who may break it. Wrenches from other mods work on JASM blocks too, and this one works with mods that accept any wrench. Recipe Four Data Crystals in a line.

Battery A Battery stores FE. It connects to adjacent machines or to a JASM network via Data Cables. Multiple batteries connect with each other to form a multiblock, granting increasing amounts of storage. At a glance (Default values) Holds 2,000,000 FE each block Size bonus 4% more FE for every battery in a multiblock Largest multiblock size 64 blocks Joining up Batteries that touch each other join as one battery and share their power. Larger multiblock sizes grant increasing power storage bonuses. A block that would join a battery past the largest size can't be placed. Charging slot A battery has one charging slot. It takes any item that holds FE and charges it from the battery's power. A bigger battery charges faster, and never faster than it has power. Breaking A broken Battery keeps its charge in the item. Breaking a block trims the rest of the battery to its new, smaller capacity. Power above it is lost. The block you mined keeps its own share. Recipe

Relay Chatterbox Two Relay Chatterboxes on the same frequency join their networks like a wireless cable. Storage, crafting and power all pass through, at any distance in the same dimension. To link across dimensions, put a Dimension Upgrade in one of the two. The dish on top turns toward its partner. Using it It is two blocks tall, so it needs room above. Join either half to a network with a Data Cable. It counts as one machine toward the machine limit. Right-click opens its screen. The frequency runs from 0 to 999: - and + change it, or type a number and press Set. Clear takes the frequency off. The Operator slot takes a Link Nibbling or a Link Byteling. Without one, the Chatterbox does nothing. The other slot takes a Dimension Upgrade. Pairs Exactly two Chatterboxes share a frequency. Your frequencies are your own: only your networks link, and a stranger can never join yours by guessing a number. A third on the same frequency waits. When one of the pair is broken or retuned, the one that has waited longest takes its place. Both blocks must be in loaded chunks. If one isn't, the link drops and comes back when it loads again. Power Every linked Chatterbox uses 200 FE per tick, or 400 FE with a Dimension Upgrade in it, even if the link stays in one dimension. The operator's battery pays. The network tops it up through the cable. One charged end is enough: it pays for both, and the power crossing the link charges the other. The link stops only when both batteries are flat, and starts again as soon as either has charge. The screen shows, top right, how much FE per tick this block is paying right now. Front light Light Meaning Green Linked, and both operators have charge. Yellow Linked, but one battery is flat. The other end pays for both. Red Not linked: no partner yet, a third one waiting, the far end not loaded, another dimension without an upgrade, or both batteries flat. Off, showing No frequency set. The screen says in words what the operator is up to. Breaking it A broken Chatterbox keeps its frequency, operator and Dimension Upgrade inside the item. Its tooltip lists them. Recipe

Data Cables Data Cables join your crafting blocks into one network and carry power between them. Any two cables join. Cables hold no power and have no speed limit. Whatever a generator or Power Interface pushes into one goes straight to the machines on the network that need it. It is made from iron, redstone and an amethyst shard, and each recipe makes 8 cables. Good to know Machines that simply touch each other form a network too, with no cable at all, and pass power on to each other like a cable. Water and other fluids can't wash a cable or its ports away. Different players' networks never join. Cables don't count toward the machine limit. See networks for the rules in full. Thin ports A cable can carry up to six thin ports, one on each face: Access Ports, item ports, Storage Ports and Power Interfaces. Breaking the cable leaves its thin ports in place, with what is in them. They stay off the network until you place a cable into the space again. Recipes

Recipe Rack A Recipe Rack holds 16 filled Recipe Cards. Every Crafting Server on the same network can use them. At a glance Holds 16 cards Uses 2 FE a tick Counts toward the machine limit Without power, the network can't see the cards inside, so autocrafting stops. Jade shows how many cards a rack holds. Processing cards go in a rack too. An Access Port lists the recipes of every rack on its network, so you pick them there. Rename a rack with the key beside its screen. The name shows in a Rack Controller and stays on the mined rack. Need more than 16 recipes? Add another rack. A Rack Controller shows them all in one panel. Recipe

Advanced Chips Rare versions of the Logic, Memory and Link Chip. Only the Chip Workshop makes them: every chip it finishes has a small chance of coming out Advanced. At a glance (Default values) Critter Chance Basic Bitling 2% Logic, Memory or Link Bitling 5% Nibbling 15% Byteling its switch picks Advanced What they are for Top-tier recipes: the Elite Deck and Elite Crafting Deck, the biggest wafers, the 64K Storage Module, the Elite Generator and Processor, the Ultimate Archive, both Bays and the Dimension Upgrade. The Ultimate Deck and Ultimate Crafting Deck need a Synapse Core. Seven of them round a Nibbling grow it into a Byteling. One of each, with a Data Crystal, builds a Synapse Core. A wild Bitling accepts one as a gift, like any other chip.

Stock Upgrade Lets an Output Port keep a block stocked instead of filling it up. Only Output and Two-Way Ports take it. Each output filter row gets a Stock number. The port tops the block up to that number and stops there. Counted over everything the row matches, in items, or mB for fluids. With a Crafting Upgrade as well, the port crafts what the blocks and your storage are short of. Recipe

Synapse Core The key to the two biggest sizes of every wafer, and to the Ultimate Deck and Ultimate Crafting Deck. A Byteling builds it in the Chip Workshop. At a glance Needs an Advanced Logic, Memory and Link Chip and a Data Crystal Builder a Byteling of any type Time 2,400 ticks, two minutes Cost 50,000 FE from the Byteling's battery Put the four ingredients in the grid in any order. Speed Upgrades in the Workshop make it faster, and it costs more power, as with chips. What it unlocks The 256K and 1M Capacity Wafers, the 128 and 256 Type Wafers, the 256K and 1M Fluid Capacity Wafers, the 64 and 128 Fluid Type Wafers, the Ultimate Deck and the Ultimate Crafting Deck. Recipe

Data Crystal The Data Crystal is JASM's basic material. You grow it on Seeded Amethyst. Mine a full cluster for Data Crystals, with your hand or any tool. Fortune gives more. Cut one into a Blank Chip at a Stonecutter. Four make a Wrench. One goes into a Synapse Core, which a Byteling builds in the Chip Workshop. Hand one to a wild Bitling and it follows you for about 30 seconds. With a book, it makes the JASM Guide.

Deployment Bay Turned off on this world. Placed bays keep their contents but don't work. A Deployment Bay places blocks, seeds and fluids from its own grid and tank into the space in front of it, as a player would. It can also throw items out, or right-click what is in front: the three keys on its panel pick Place, Drop or Interact. At a glance Speed 3 seconds, down to 0.2 seconds with 4 Speed Upgrades Cost 20 FE for each block, fluid, stack or click Upgrades five slots: up to four Speed Upgrades and one Redstone Upgrade Holds 10,000 FE and 16 buckets Good to know Its Input / Output key opens sides for items and fluids separately, each Input or closed. An Output Port, hopper or pipe fills it through a side set to Input. A new bay takes things in on every side except its front. It runs on cable power and doesn't take up a place on the machine limit. It also takes power from any cable or pipe, other mods' too: the Energy tab of its Input / Output key sets which sides take it. Speed Upgrades raise the power per action as well as the speed. Four upgrades cost two and a half times the power for each action. With a Redstone Upgrade it can run only while powered or unpowered, or work once for each redstone pulse. In interact mode it right-clicks the block or mob in front with what is in its top-left grid slot, or an empty hand. It never places blocks, and tools wear down as in your hand. What the click gives goes into its other slots; what doesn't fit is thrown out. In drop mode items land in the middle of the space in front of the bay, or on top of or beside a solid block there. It pauses while 32 entities are near, so it can't flood a spot with items. You can add filters to decide what it may or may not place/drop. Works for items and fluids. Its opposite is the Demolition Bay. Recipe

Networks Machines that are joined by Data Cables form a network. So do JASM machines that simply touch each other, with no cable at all. What counts as a machine A network can only hold so many machines. The Network Brain page has the numbers. Everything that does a job counts: Network Encoders, Recipe Racks and Crafting Servers. Access Ports and every other port. Archives. Chip Workshops, Crystal Foundries and Bitling Stations. Cables, generators, Creative Batteries, brains and chambers don't count. Neither do the two bays and the Crystal Resonator. A row of five Archives side by side is a network of five. Who may use it The network belongs to the player who set it up. The owner can trust other players at a Network Encoder. Trusted players can use the blocks and Archives on that network. Different players' networks never join. See co-op play for everything you can share. Seeing the network A linked Deck has a Network tab. It lists every machine, generator and Battery with the power each adds or uses, grouped by category or as one list. Power Cables carry power too, and so do machines that touch each other. A tower of machines needs only one cable. See power.

Blank Upgrade An upgrade with nothing on it yet. It is the base of the other upgrades. The Speed, Redstone, Power, Crafting and Stock Upgrades are each crafted from one. The Dimension Upgrade is crafted from a Redstone Upgrade. Recipe

Settings Every number and switch JASM lets you change, in the order the config screen shows them. Changing a value Choose Mods, JASM, Config. The sections are on the left and each setting has a short description. The screen has two parts: My settings ( ) and World rules ( ). My settings can always be changed. World rules can be changed in singleplayer and by operators on a server. Everyone else sees them locked, and with no world open they show the normal values. A changed value turns yellow and gets a Reset key. Reset section puts the open section back to its defaults. A value outside its range can't be saved. Changes are saved when you press Done. When a change applies Settings marked Needs restart (Deck slots, the features and the Basic Bitling recipe) apply after the world reloads, or after the server restarts. The rest apply at once. Players who join a server get the server's world rules. A server's can also be edited by hand. Where the values are kept Each world keeps its own copy, at. The copy in is only what new worlds start with. An update never changes a value that is already saved in a file. An old world keeps its old numbers until you change them. World rules These are in. Crafting Server The Crafting Server does the work. It runs one crafting job at a time. Processors decide how many crafts run at once, and Storage Modules decide how big a job fits. At a glance Slots 4 for Processors, 4 for Storage Modules Uses what its Processors use, only while it has a job. Nothing when idle Each craft takes half a second, whatever the Processor Counts toward the machine limit Good to know Its parts are locked in while it works. Broken, it spills whatever its job held. The Advanced Crafting Server is a bigger one with ten slots of each. The screen shows what the job is waiting for: power, a card, space or the Deck, no Access Port serving the recipe, or what a machine is doing: waiting for it to take the items (in yellow), not loaded, unreachable, unpowered, paused by redstone or in use by another job. A machine that is only busy or slow shows nothing. The magnifier key lights up the machine in the world. A job can be cancelled. What is left comes back. Which server gets a job With several servers on a network, a job goes to one that fits and is free. A Crafting Deck's request window can pick one by name instead, and the Deck keeps that pick for its next requests. The rename key gives a server a name. A mined server keeps its name. The star key makes it a priority server. Ports with a Crafting Upgrade send their crafts to priority servers first, and use the others when those are busy. How a craft runs See autocrafting. Recipe

Crafting rules A rule makes the network craft for you, without you asking. Set them on the Rules tab of a Crafting Deck. Two kinds Rule Example Fewer than when I have fewer than 16 torches, craft 32 Every every minute, craft 8 bread Pick the item by holding it and clicking. A timer can be no shorter than 10 seconds. Where it goes Choose where the results go: onto the Deck, or straight into your inventory. A "fewer than" rule counts what you carry when it sends to you. Good to know A rule runs one job at a time. If a job can't start, the rule waits 5 seconds and tries again. The rule's line says why. Each rule can be switched on or off. The rules need the same chain as autocrafting: recipe cards, a rack, a server.

Seeded Amethyst Seeded Amethyst is a Block of Amethyst with a Crystal Seed in it. It grows Data Crystal buds on its open sides, like budding amethyst. Buds grow in four steps: Small Data Crystal Bud, Medium Data Crystal Bud, Large Data Crystal Bud, then a full Data Crystal Cluster. Mine the cluster for Data Crystal. Fortune gives more. A bud broken early gives Crystal Dust instead. Each time a bud grows, the block may wear down: Seeded, Worn Seeded Amethyst, Cracked Seeded Amethyst, then a plain Block of Amethyst. Mined at any stage, it gives the Block of Amethyst back and the seed is lost. A powered Crystal Resonator makes it grow faster. Growing crystals draw wild Bitlings. See befriending them. More in Growing Data Crystals.

Override Link A Network Encoder links Decks for the whole network. An Archive links one player's Deck for itself alone, with its Override Link window. Network link and Archive link The Deck Link window on a Network Encoder pairs a player's Deck with the network. A paired Deck gets the Network tab, autocrafting, ports and Deck to Deck. An Archive backs up the owner's Deck. The Override Link window changes that for this Archive only, and not for the network or any other Archive. Overriding an Archive Trust the player at a Network Encoder and have them pair their Deck there. Open the Archive and press the Override Link key on its right. Put their Deck in the left slot and take it from the right. Only that player can then back up and recover on this Archive. The owner and the other trusted players can look. Picking another player clears the backups. Going back Reset gives the Archive back to the owner's Deck. Resetting from another player's Deck clears the backups. Good to know Only the owner can override an Archive. The key is dimmed while the owner is the only player on the network. Trust someone first. Replace a lost Deck for the same player and the backups stay.

Dimension Upgrade A Deck works only in the Overworld until you give it this. Install one in the Deck's upgrade slot and it works in the Nether, the End and modded dimensions too. What else it covers The same limit applies to linked ports, crafting jobs and rules. They pause when the Deck, or its network, is outside the Overworld without the upgrade. The upgrade slot stays open, so you can always fix it. Sending items to a player in another dimension needs the upgrade on both Decks. See sending items. Two Relay Chatterboxes link across dimensions when either one holds this upgrade. Recipe

Bitlings Bitlings are small robot helpers that work the Chip Workshop. Without one, a Workshop does nothing. Wild Bitlings Hand one a typed chip to get a Basic Bitling item. Hand one a Data Crystal and it follows you for a while. Hand one a diamond and it leaves a Block of Amethyst. Knocked out, it leaves one or two Crystal Dust. Basic Bitling Find a wild Bitling and hand it a chip. On this world you can also craft one: Makes Logic, Memory and Link Chips evenly, and rarely an Advanced one. Battery of 50,000 FE. The Network Brain recipe needs one. Typed Bitlings Surround a Basic Bitling with 8 chips of one type in a crafting grid to get a Logic, Memory or Link Bitling. Mostly makes its own type, sometimes Advanced. Battery of 150,000 FE. Trains on every chip it makes, then grows into a Nibbling. Changing type A Logic, Memory or Link Bitling, Nibbling or Byteling turns into another type of the same stage. Put it in the middle of a crafting grid and surround it with eight chips of the new type: Logic, Memory or Link Chips, or the Advanced ones for a Byteling. It keeps its charge. Its training starts again from zero. Recipes

Getting started Everything JASM stores lives on wafers. Put wafers in a Deck and carry it with you. Link the Deck to a powered Archive to keep backups, so a lost wafer can be rebuilt onto a blank one. To open this guide at any time, craft the JASM Guide. A first hour Grow Data Crystals on a block of amethyst. Cut them into chips by hand. Craft your first Capacity Wafer and a Starter Deck. Build a Chip Workshop and befriend a wild Bitling to work in it. Link Chips come only from there. How the tiers use the chips The first tier of every wafer, Deck, generator and cable is made from vanilla items. From there on, recipes use JASM's own chips. Every higher tier needs the tier below it, and nothing it holds is lost on the way up. Where next Mechanics: how the systems work. Items, blocks and machines: one page for each, with recipes.

Power Interface JASM blocks only take power from JASM generators, batteries and cables. The Power Interface is the way in for power from other mods, and the way out for JASM power. Put it between the other mod's power and a Data Cable or machine. Right-click it to pick what it does: Input only: it accepts the FE other mods push into it and feeds the cables and machines it touches. It never pulls power out of anything, and only takes what the machines and Batteries on its network have room for. This is the default. Output only: it gives power from Batteries first: Batteries it touches, and Batteries on its network, in every dimension the network reaches. With no battery, or once all are empty, it draws from Combustion Generators touching it or the network's cables. It never takes the power inside machines. In Output only, it feeds every block it touches that takes power, from other mods or JASM, except blocks on a network it draws power from. A Bay is fed through its Energy tab faces. Its screen shows the power going through it, in FE/t. At a glance Speed set by the other mod: it holds no power and passes on whatever is pushed into it, as far as the network has room Direction set in its screen: Input only or Output only The cable-mounted Power Interface does the same from a cable face, like a thin Access Port: its plate faces out, and it only trades power with the block in front of it. Its mode is set the same way, in its screen. Craft either form on its own to turn it into the other. If you only need to charge a Deck, a Combustion Generator is simpler. Recipe

Crafting Upgrade A port with a Crafting Upgrade asks your Crafting Deck to craft what it is sending out. Only Output and Two-Way Ports take it. It crafts what the port's output filter allows, when you have a recipe card for it. It looks once a second and runs one job at a time. With a Stock Upgrade it only crafts what the blocks and your storage are short of. Without one it keeps crafting a stack at a time while the ingredients last. Recipe

Bitling Station Put a Bitling, Nibbling or Byteling in a Bitling Station and a little living copy pops out. It walks, sprints, looks about and lies down for a rest. Right-click it to pet it. Power The little Bitling is only a body. The critter's own battery pays for the walk: 5 FE a tick while it is out and about. When the battery drops to 5%, it walks home and sits on the pad. The station passes the power it gets straight into the critter's battery. Connect the station to a Data Cable network or put a generator next to it. Stuck on the way home, or out of charge? It teleports back onto the pad. Good to know The screen shows what it is doing, its battery and a slider for how far it may roam (4 to 16 blocks). If something knocks it out, it comes back after 30 seconds with full health. Take the critter out and the little Bitling is gone. Hoppers and pipes can't reach the critter slot. Only the owner and the players they trust can open the station. A Bitling Station counts toward a network's machine limit. Recipe

JASM Guide The JASM Guide is the book you are reading now. Right-click it to open the guide. Hold the guide key (G by default) over any item's tooltip to jump to that item's page. You don't need the book for this. Recipe

Access Port The Access Port is how your network talks to other machines. Put one next to a furnace, a modded machine or a multiblock, then pick which processing recipes it makes there. Setting it up Join the port to your network with a Data Cable. Write a processing recipe at a Network Encoder: what goes in, and up to three things that come back. Keep the card in a Recipe Rack. Right-click the port and pick the recipe in its screen. Make the machine give its results back into the port, or use a hopper or a pipe. A JASM machine with an Input / Output key works with the port only through the side facing it: Input takes the ingredients, Output sends the results back into the port. Fluids work too. Several ports with the same recipe share the work. The port screen Recipe list on the left: every processing recipe in the Recipe Racks of your network. Search it by name, hover a recipe for its details, and fold the list away with the key on its left edge. Active recipes on the main panel: the ones this port makes, up to 16. Click a recipe in the list to add it, click it in the active bar to remove it. A tick in the list marks recipes the port already serves. Machine row: the machine the port works with, and what it is doing. Hover its icon for the name. A recipe whose card has left every rack is dimmed and marked as missing. It comes back when the card is in a rack again. The pencil key opens a small window to rename the port. Press Rename to set the name. Copy and Paste keys on the Active recipes row remember a port's name and recipes until the game closes. Click Paste to replace this port's name and recipes, or Shift+click to add its recipes (up to 16). Editing a card makes a new recipe: pick the new one again. Machine types A full block port works with the kinds of machine picked in its Machine row, even if others touch it. The first one it finds is picked. When more kinds are touching, click their icons to pick or unpick them; one always stays picked. If the machine is swapped for another kind, the port follows once the old kind is gone. With several machines picked, even of different kinds, a job splits its sets evenly between all of them. Make sure each one can run the recipe: a job waits for a machine that won't take its share. A thin port has one machine, the one it faces. Only one port works with a machine. A second port facing a machine another port already uses does nothing with it, and its screen says "Machine in use by another port". It takes the machine over when the first port is broken or turned away. Active and Passive The key at the start of the Machine row switches a full block port between Active and Passive. It can't be switched while a job is using the port. Active sends each set of ingredients straight into the picked machines. Passive has no machines. Each set waits hidden inside the port, and pipes or hoppers pull it out from any face. They can take only those ingredients, never the incoming items or the network's storage. Push the results back into the port to finish the set. A Passive port holds up to nine stacks of items, plus the fluids of its sets, and works on one recipe at a time. With Blocking Mode on, the next set waits until the last one's results are back. Recipes with other mods' materials don't run through it. Cancelling a job takes back what is still waiting in the port; what the pipes already took is yours. Breaking the port sends what it holds to the network, or drops the items when it has none. Two shapes Full block: also takes items from any face, even without a crafting job. It has an eight-slot buffer. Ordinary items go to the owner's paired Deck, or to another paired Deck you pick in the port. Items wait if the Deck is full. Thin: a cable attachment, up to six on one cable, one per face. It can also sit straight on a machine with no cable. It stays off the network until you place a cable into its space, and it stays in place if the cable is broken. Convert one into the other in a crafting

Fluid Capacity Wafers The same idea as a Capacity Wafer, for fluids. It holds any mix of fluids, counted in buckets: one bucket takes the room of one item. Wafer Holds, in buckets Needs Basic 256 vanilla items only 1K 1,024 Memory Chip 4K 4,096 Memory Chip 16K 16,384 Memory Chip and Link Chip 64K 65,536 Advanced Memory Chip 256K 262,144 Synapse Core 1M 1,048,576 Synapse Core Every size is made from three wafers of the size below. They are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their fluid and starts unlinked. The 256K and 1M sizes need Synapse Cores. Using them They go in any Deck slot, next to item wafers. The Deck's grid shows items and fluids together. A button shows only one kind. Right-click the grid with a full bucket, or shift-right-click it in your inventory, to pour it in. Click a fluid with an empty bucket to fill it. A Crafting Deck can also place and collect fluids in the world, like a bucket. Input and Output Ports move fluids too. See item ports. Recipes

Crystal Dust Crystal Dust is what a bud gives when you break it before it is fully grown. A wild Bitling that gets knocked out leaves one or two as well. Four dust and a redstone make a Crystal Seed. Buds are the early stages of Seeded Amethyst. Recipe

Archives An Archive keeps a backup of your wafers. If one is ever lost or destroyed, the Archive rebuilds it onto a blank wafer, items and all. Tier Wafers it protects Charge Uses Basic 3 50,000 FE 5 FE a tick Advanced 6 100,000 FE 10 FE a tick Ultimate 12 200,000 FE 20 FE a tick An Archive needs power to link or recover, so give it a cable or a generator next to it. At a glance Linking a wafer 1,000 FE Recovering a wafer 10,000 FE Using one Put a wafer in the link slot and press Link. Shift-right-click with the linked Deck to back up all its wafers in slot order. To recover a lost wafer, put a blank one of the same kind in the recover slot and press Recover. To back up another player's Deck instead of yours, see Override Link. The blank wafer has to be the same size or bigger than the one it replaces. Upgrading The old Archive is used up. The new one keeps its links, its owner and its charge. Recipes

Autocrafting Ask for anything from your Crafting Deck, and the network crafts what it needs first. What you need A Crafting Deck, paired at a Network Encoder. Recipe Cards for the recipes, kept in a Recipe Rack. A Crafting Server with a Processor and a Storage Module. A Data Cable network that joins them, with power. For a machine instead of a crafting table, write a processing card and add an Access Port. Open the port and pick the recipe there. Several ports with the same recipe share the work. Asking for something Open the Craft tab on the Deck, pick an item and an amount, and press Craft. The Deck works out the steps and shows: Makes: what you get. Crafts first: the steps in between, as a list or a tree. Missing: anything it can't find. The amount box takes a sum: type to craft 150. It understands, does times and divide first, and rounds a divide down. The answer shows beside the box, and Craft stays off while it is not a whole number from 1 to 9999999. Crafting rules take the same sums in their craft box. A hammer in the Items tab marks items with a known recipe, even when some are already stored. Items a recipe hands back, like Mystical Agriculture's Infusion Crystals, are reused: one copy serves every craft in the job, even if it is enchanted or renamed. While it runs Requested items come back as each batch finishes. Items made along the way stay with the job until it ends. A job list on the Deck shows every job. Click one to open its server from anywhere. A job whose recipe no Access Port serves waits, and says "No Access Port serving recipe". It carries on once a port picks the recipe. Cancel a job and what is left comes back. When it says no The Deck tells you why: Missing ingredients. No Recipe Card makes that. No server with a Processor, or every fitting server is busy. The job is too big for the Storage Modules. The network is full. Add a Network Brain. The biggest request is 100,000 items. See also crafting rules.

Network Brain A network holds only machines on its own. A Network Brain lifts that to, and with Network Chamber s round it, a lot more. Brain Machines Uses each tick Holds No brain Lone brain 8 FE 50,000 FE 1 floor 24 FE 145,000 FE 2 floors 52 FE 310,000 FE 3 floors 110 FE 660,000 FE 4 floors 240 FE 1,450,000 FE 5 floors 510 FE 3,050,000 FE 6 floors 1,100 FE 6,600,000 FE 7 floors 2,300 FE 13,800,000 FE 8 floors 5,000 FE 30,000,000 FE The rules Add a machine past the limit and the whole network stops, until you remove one or add a brain. A brain uses power every tick, and a taller tower uses more. If it runs out, the network falls back to machines. A whole tower shares one pool of power. A cable on any of its floors or chambers fills it, and its screen shows the pool and what the tower uses each tick. Mined, a brain keeps its charge. Several brains on one network don't add up. Only the best one leads, the one with the most floors, then the one placed first. The machines' screens and Jade say when a network is full, and a linked Deck's Network tab shows the count. See what counts as a machine. Floors and towers Put 8 Network Chambers round a brain on the same layer to make a floor. Stack floors into a tower. All of that is on the Network Chamber page. Recipe The recipe needs a Basic Bitling. Befriend a wild one first.

Speed Upgrade Makes a port, a bay, the Crystal Foundry or the Chip Workshop work faster. At a glance (Default values) Speed Upgrades Speed Power per job 0 normal normal 1 2x 1.25x 2 4x 1.5x 3 8x 2x 4 16x 2.5x All of them have five upgrade slots, and a machine takes at most four Speed Upgrades. The other slots are for other upgrades, like the Redstone Upgrade. The Deployment and Demolition Bays, the Crystal Foundry and the Chip Workshop share one rule: each upgrade doubles the speed, and every job costs a bit more power. In the Workshop this counts for chips and for the Synapse Core alike. A port with four of them moves 96 items every operation, up from 1. See item ports and the Access Port. Ports use no power themselves, with or without upgrades. The Deck they move items in and out of pays 1 FE for each item, as usual. Upgrades stack normally in your inventory and in storage. Recipe

Rack Controller A Rack Controller shows every Recipe Rack on its network in one panel. It joins the network like any other crafting block. At a glance (Default values) Uses 2 FE a tick The panel Each rack has a section with its name and its 16 slots. A rack with no name shows as Recipe Rack. Hover a name to see where the rack stands. Click a card to take it. Click an empty slot to put the card you hold in. Shift-click a card to send it to your inventory, or a written card in your inventory to put it in the first free slot. The search box finds cards by what they make. Racks with no match fold up to their name. Racks in other dimensions joined by a far link are listed too. Racks in unloaded chunks are not. You only see the racks you may use. Power Without power the panel lists no racks. The controller counts toward the machine limit. Recipe

Infinite Wafers An Infinite Water Wafer or Infinite Lava Wafer goes in a Deck like any fluid wafer and holds only its own fluid, without end. At a glance (Default values) Amount shown 1,000,000,000 buckets Power per bucket moved 8 FE Using one The Deck always shows the same amount of its fluid. Taking some out never lowers it. Buckets, tanks, ports, pipes and crafting jobs can all take from it. Water or lava put into the Deck goes to its infinite wafer first and is deleted. This costs charge like any other move. Water or lava already on other wafers, or in tanks lent by a Storage Port, stays where it is. It has no filters. Pull all Right-click an infinite wafer in the Deck's wafer panel to open its small window. Pull all deletes all of its fluid stored on the Deck's other wafers. It costs charge like moving that fluid, 8 FE per bucket. Without charge for all of it, it pulls as many whole buckets as the charge pays for and says Out of charge. The emptied wafers keep their settings and name. Tanks lent by a Storage Port are left alone. The window shows how much was pulled. Recipes

How storage works Your items don't sit inside a wafer. The wafer is a key, and the items live in the world's records under that wafer's number. That is why a wafer is safe to carry, and why it can be rebuilt. The pieces Wafers hold the items. See Capacity and Type Wafers. Decks carry the wafers and give you a screen to use them. See Decks. Archives keep backups, so a lost wafer can be recovered. See Archives. Safe by design A copied wafer stops working. It is wiped blank, and the original is untouched. A wafer that is older than the records say, or from another world, is locked. It keeps its contents and does nothing until it can be matched up again. A crash never duplicates items. Items from a mod you removed are kept until the mod comes back. What a wafer won't take Items that hold other items, like a full shulker box. Items that carry too much data to save. Items that can't be saved at all. The Deck's screen says why when it turns something away.

Crystal Seed A Crystal Seed turns a Block of Amethyst into Seeded Amethyst, which grows Data Crystal. Use it on a Block of Amethyst. The seed is used up (not in creative mode). The Crystal Foundry also takes seeds, and makes Blank Chips from them. You can make a seed from amethyst, wheat seeds and redstone, or from four Crystal Dust and a redstone. More in Growing Data Crystals. Recipes

Sending items to players Turned off on this world. Nothing new can be sent. Trips already on their way still arrive, and the inbox can still be emptied. Deck to Deck sends items to another player on your network, or on any network whose owner trusts you. They travel for a while, then land in the other player's inbox. How to send Pair your Deck at a Network Encoder, or ask a network's owner to trust you. Press Deck to Deck on the Deck's screen and choose a player. Only players online on your network, or on a network whose owner trusts you, show up. Put the items in the send grid and press Send. When the owner stops trusting you, you can't send to their network any more, even from a Deck you paired there. The grid is 1 slot on a Starter Deck, 3 on a Basic, 6 on an Advanced and 9 on Elite and Ultimate. The trip At a glance Charge twice what the same items would cost to move Travel time 5 seconds, plus about 1 second for every 64 blocks Other dimension 30 seconds more Longest trip 10 minutes Trips at once 10 Call back returns the items to your own inbox. The inbox Items land in the inbox. Store all moves them onto your Deck. If the inbox is full, the trip waits there until there is room. Sending to another dimension needs a Dimension Upgrade on both Decks.

Storage Port A Storage Port lends the chest, tank or cauldron in front of it to the whole network. Everything inside shows up in a linked Deck next to the wafers, marked with a small chest. Take it out or put it in like wafer storage. Two shapes Thin: sits on a Data Cable face and lends the block in front of it. Block: joins the network like a machine and lends every chest, tank or cauldron it touches, all with the same settings. Convert one shape into the other in a crafting grid. Settings Filter: see Type Filters. Access: read and write, read only or write only. Priority: higher priority takes things in first and the lowest is emptied first. Wafers go first on a tie. Anyone allowed on the network can use it. Recipe A Storage Port is an Access Port with a chest, a Link Chip and purple dye.

Combustion Generators Turned off on this world. Placed generators keep their fuel and charge but don't burn. Burn anything a furnace burns and get power. A generator charges Decks and other chargeable items in its charging slot first, then sends what is left into every block it touches. Tier Burns Makes Holds Gives per block Basic 2x faster 40 FE a tick 100,000 FE 1,000 FE a tick Advanced 4x faster 160 FE a tick 400,000 FE 2,500 FE a tick Elite 6x faster 480 FE a tick 1,000,000 FE 5,000 FE a tick A piece of coal gives 32,000 FE in a Basic generator over 40 seconds, 64,000 FE over 20 seconds in an Advanced one and 127,680 FE over 13.3 seconds in an Elite one. Tips Put one next to a Chip Workshop or an Archive to power it without any cable. Drop a Deck in the charging slot to top up its battery. Jade shows how long the fuel has left. Upgrading The old generator is used up. The new one keeps its stored power. Recipes A server can turn off the Elite generator. Elite generators already placed don't burn, and keep their fuel and charge.

Co-op play Friends can share one network. Everyone keeps their own Deck and their own wafers, while the network shares its machines, recipes and chests. Who owns what A network belongs to the player who set it up. A machine or cable placed onto it joins it and belongs to the network's owner, whoever placed it. Two players' networks never join. A cable placed between them stays on its own. Trusting friends Open a Network Encoder on your network. Open its Access window and type a friend's name. They don't have to be online. Stop trusting takes them off the list again. Only the owner can trust players, up to 32 per encoder. Trusted players can open and use every JASM machine and Archive on that network. Everyone else is turned away, even if they join a cable to it. Pairing your own Deck Each trusted player pairs their own Deck at the encoder, in the Deck Link window. It is one Deck per player: pairing another replaces your old one. A paired Deck gets the Network tab, autocrafting, ports and Deck to Deck. Placing the first Network Encoder on a network of your own pairs a Deck you carry, unless it is already paired somewhere. What you share and what you keep Shared by everyone Your own Recipe Cards, Recipe Racks and Crafting Servers the wafers in your Deck chests and tanks behind Storage Ports your Deck's charge the machine limit and the power your inbox Crafting together A craft started from your Deck takes its ingredients from your own wafers, and the result comes back to you. The recipes, racks, servers and processors belong to the network, so everyone crafts with the same setup. See autocrafting. Ports Item Ports and full Access Ports work with the owner's Deck at first. A trusted player can put their own paired Deck in the port's Deck Link window, and the port works with that Deck instead. Archives On a network, an Archive backs up the owner's Deck. The owner can link a trusted player's paired Deck instead. Only that player can then back up and recover; the other trusted players can look. Picking another player clears the backups. See Override Link. Sending items Deck to Deck sends items to any online player whose Deck is paired on the same network, or on any network whose owner trusts you. When the owner stops trusting you, that stops at once. See sending items to players. Good to know The Network tab shows the same machines to everyone who is trusted. JASM doesn't stop other players breaking your blocks. On a public server, use a land claim mod for that.

Backups and recovery Link a wafer to an Archive and it can be recovered if it is lost. Backing up Place an Archive and give it power. Shift-right-click it with your Deck. The Deck's wafers are backed up in slot order. Wafers already backed up on the network are skipped, and the Archive's free slots decide how many fit. The screen shows how many wafers are backed up. Recovering Put a blank wafer of the same kind in the recover slot and press Recover. The new wafer gets everything the lost one held. It has to be the same size or bigger. Who can use an Archive A standalone Archive works for its owner with no Network Encoder. It links the Deck in the owner's hand on the first backup. On a network, it defaults to the network owner. The owner can pick another trusted player's Deck instead, with Override Link. Trusted players can look at the backups. Replace a lost Deck for the same player and the backups stay.

Type Wafers A Type Wafer holds only a few kinds of item, but a huge amount of each. Pick one for the things you collect by the thousand, like cobblestone. Wafer Each type holds Needs 4 types 2,048 vanilla items only 8 types 8,192 Memory Chip 16 types 32,768 Memory Chip 32 types 131,072 Link Chip 64 types 524,288 Advanced Memory Chip 128 types 2,097,152 Synapse Core 256 types 8,388,608 Synapse Core What counts as a type A type follows vanilla stacking. Items that don't stack, like tools and armour, each take a whole type to themselves. Save the Type Wafers for stackable things. Upgrading Every size is made from two wafers of the size before. They are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their items and starts unlinked. The 128 and 256 sizes need Synapse Cores. For fluids, see Fluid Type Wafers. Recipes

Chip Workshop Put a Bitling in the Chip Workshop and feed it Blank Chip s. It turns them into Logic, Memory and Link Chip s, and now and then a rare Advanced Logic Chip. At a glance Time per chip 8 seconds Time with 4 Speed Upgrades 0.5 seconds Cost 2,000 FE from the Bitling's battery for every chip Cost with 4 Speed Upgrades 5,000 FE for every chip Input a 2x2 grid Upgrades five slots: up to four Speed Upgrades and one Redstone Upgrade Who makes what Critter Makes Basic Bitling all three types evenly, rarely an Advanced one Logic, Memory or Link Bitling mostly its own type, sometimes Advanced Logic Nibbling only its own type, Advanced more often Logic Byteling only its own type; a switch picks standard or Advanced Power The Workshop itself uses no power. Only the critter does. Power from a cable or a generator next to it goes straight into the critter's battery, as fast as they can give it. It makes one chip at a time. A chip starts once the battery holds its whole cost, and the critter pays a little every tick while it works, nothing while it waits. Each Speed Upgrade doubles the speed, and every chip costs a bit more. With no power at all, the critter keeps going until it can't pay for another chip, then naps until it has enough for one. A half-made chip keeps its progress through a nap. You can also charge a critter in a Combustion Generator. A Redstone Upgrade adds a key under the upgrade slots to pause the Workshop. The critter still charges while it waits, and a half-made chip keeps its progress. Building things in the grid Blank Chips can go in any of the four slots, and the critter keeps making chips even with other things beside them. A few things aren't chips: a Byteling builds the Synapse Core from what is in the grid. Its Input / Output key sets each side and shows the block next to it. Input fills the grid. Output lets finished chips be pulled out there. The Blank Chips in the grid never leave through a side. Every side starts at Input. With Auto Output on, the Workshop also sends finished chips out of its Output sides into whatever is there, an Access Port included. It starts off. For Access Port jobs, set the side facing the port to Input/Output and turn Auto Output on. A Chip Workshop counts toward a network's machine limit. Recipe

Item ports Ports move items and fluids between the network and the blocks next to them. Port Does Input Port pulls into a linked Deck Output Port pushes out of the Deck Two-Way Port both, with output first Two shapes Thin: sits on a Data Cable face and works on the block in front of it. Block: joins the network like a machine and works on every block it touches, with one set of filters and one speed shared between them. On a JASM machine, a block port only moves what that face's I/O setting allows. Machines, hoppers and pipes can push items and fluids into an Input or Two-Way Port, and they go into the network's storage when there's room. A thin one takes them only through its outward face. Convert one shape into the other in a crafting grid. Filters Each direction has its own filter. An empty output filter sends nothing. A Two-Way Port shows one at a time: the Output and Input buttons switch between them. Speed Ports run twice a second while they are busy, and check once a second after five idle seconds. Five upgrade slots take up to four Speed Upgrades. Upgrades Items per operation Items per second 0 1 2 1 4 8 2 16 32 3 48 96 4 96 192 Fluids share that speed with items. More slots A Power Upgrade makes the port supply FE to the machine it faces. A Redstone Upgrade makes it follow a redstone signal. On Output and Two-Way Ports, a Crafting Upgrade crafts what the port sends and a Stock Upgrade keeps a block stocked to a number. Recipes An Input or Output Port is an Access Port with a hopper or dropper, a Link Chip and a dye.

Redstone Upgrade Lets redstone switch a machine on and off. Put it in one of the machine's upgrade slots. A machine takes one. Machines that take it Input, Output and Two-Way item ports, thin or block. Access Ports, thin or block. The Crystal Foundry. The Chip Workshop. The Deployment Bay and the Demolition Bay. Modes A redstone key shows up on the machine's screen once the upgrade is in. It picks one of three: Ignore redstone. Run while powered. Run while unpowered. The bays have a fourth: work once for each redstone pulse. Good to know Take the upgrade out and the machine runs normally again. A paused machine keeps its progress. A Foundry keeps its crystal, a Workshop its half-made chips. The Workshop's critter still charges. A paused Access Port moves nothing to its machine or back, and crafting jobs wait for it. A port's mode controls both directions at once. All ports in the same block space get the same redstone signal. Each one follows its own mode. A port with no upgrade keeps running. Recipe

Crystal Foundry The Crystal Foundry grows Data Crystals in bulk and cuts each one into a Blank Chip. A Crystal Seed grows into Blank Chips. The seed is used up as soon as it starts growing. It runs on power from a Data Cable network or a generator next to it. Five upgrade slots take up to four Speed Upgrades and one Redstone Upgrade. It waits when its outputs are full. A Redstone Upgrade adds a key under the slots to pause it, and the crystal keeps its progress. It counts toward a network's machine limit. See the Network Brain. Sides and output Its Input / Output key sets each side and shows the block next to it. Input lets hoppers and pipes put seeds in. Output lets the chips be pulled out there. Every side starts at Input. With Auto Output on, it also sends the chips out of its Output sides into whatever is there, an Access Port included. It starts off. For Access Port jobs, set the side facing the port to Input/Output and turn Auto Output on. At a glance (Default values) Chips per seed 16 Time per chip 8 seconds Power use 50 FE/t Power use with 1 Speed Upgrade 125 FE/t Power use with 2 Speed Upgrades 300 FE/t Power use with 3 Speed Upgrades 800 FE/t Power use with 4 Speed Upgrades 2,000 FE/t Recipe

Blank Chip A Blank Chip is a Data Crystal cut flat. Every other chip starts as one. The Crystal Foundry makes them straight from Crystal Seeds. Cook one to start a Logic or Memory Chip. See Making chips by hand. A Bitling in the Chip Workshop turns Blank Chips into Logic, Memory and Link Chips, and sometimes Advanced ones. See Chip Workshop. Recipe

Processors Processors go in a Crafting Server. Each one runs crafts side by side, so more Processors means a job finishes sooner. Processor Cores Uses while its server has a job Basic 1 10 FE a tick Advanced 4 30 FE a tick Elite 16 80 FE a tick Every tier crafts at the same speed. A higher tier just does more of them at once. One Processor also handles a processing job: it keeps one set out in a machine until the results come back. With all Processors busy, a job waits, even if other machines are free. Making one Each tier is made from four of the tier below. The Advanced Processor also needs a Link Chip and the Elite an Advanced Logic Chip. Recipes

Items, blocks and machines One page for each item, block and machine, with its recipe. Hold the guide key over an item to jump to its page. The pages are in the order you will meet them. Crystals and chips JASM Guide: the book you are reading. Crystal Seed: turns amethyst into a crystal farm. Seeded Amethyst: where Data Crystals grow. Data Crystal: the raw material. Crystal Dust: what a bud broken early leaves. Crystal Resonator: makes crystals and plants grow faster. Crystal Foundry: grows crystals in bulk. Blank Chip: cut from a Data Crystal. Logic and Memory Chips: the parts of every recipe. Bitlings and the Workshop Chip Workshop: a Bitling turns Blank Chips into better ones. Bitling Station: a home for your Bitling. Bitlings: the helpers. Nibblings and Bytelings: the grown-up stages. Link Chip: for the third tier. Advanced Chips: rare, for the top tier. Synapse Core: unlocks the biggest wafers and the Ultimate Decks. Storage Capacity Wafers: any mix of items. Type Wafers: a few kinds, in bulk. Fluid Capacity Wafers: any mix of fluids. Fluid Type Wafers: a few fluids, in bulk. Infinite Wafers: water or lava that never runs out. Decks: the handheld reader. Crafting Decks: a Deck with a crafting grid. Dimension Upgrade: use a Deck outside the Overworld. Archives: backups for your wafers. Network and power Data Cables: join machines and carry power. Power Interface: moves power between a network and other mods' blocks. Combustion Generators: burn fuel for power. Battery: stores power and joins up with its neighbours. Network Brain: lifts the machine limit. Network Chamber: builds brain floors and towers. Relay Chatterbox: links two networks like a wireless cable. Network Tether: keeps every chunk of its network loaded. Ports and bays Access Port: talks to other machines. Item ports: move items and fluids in and out of a Deck. Storage Port: lends a chest or tank to the network. Docking Station: lets the network use a Deck while its owner is away. Blank Upgrade: the base for other upgrades. Speed Upgrade, Redstone Upgrade and Power Upgrade. Crafting Upgrade and Stock Upgrade: for Output Ports. Deployment Bay: places blocks and fluids. Demolition Bay: breaks blocks. Wrench: turn machines and pick them up. Autocrafting Network Encoder: writes recipes and pairs Decks. Advanced Encoder: a Network Encoder that picks which face of a machine each ingredient goes in through. Recipe Cards: hold one recipe each. Material: stands for another mod's material on a card. Recipe Rack: stores 16 cards. Rack Controller: every rack's cards in one panel. Crafting Server: runs the jobs. Advanced Crafting Server: the same with room for ten of everything. Processors: how many crafts run at once. Storage Modules: how big a job fits.

Network Tether Keeps every chunk its network touches loaded, even with nobody near: every cable and machine, and both ends of a Relay Chatterbox link. A Nibbling or Byteling keeps watch at its desk. At a glance (Default values) Cost with 1 chunk 81 FE/t Cost with 9 chunks 125 FE/t Cost with 25 chunks 405 FE/t Chunks kept after the power runs out 10 seconds Using it Join it to a network with a Data Cable. It doesn't count toward the machine limit. The Operator slot takes any Nibbling or Byteling. Without one, nothing is kept loaded. The operator's battery pays. The network tops it up through the cable. Each chunk held costs a little more than the one before. With several Tethers on one network, the one placed first keeps watch and the others stand by. One standing by takes over if it stops. Good to know The chunks stay loaded while you are away, and after a restart. Mobs spawn in them as they do near a player. When the battery runs flat, the chunks are let go a few seconds later. Take the operator out and they are let go at once. A chunk is only known once a cable or machine in it has been loaded with the Tether in place. A server can switch Tethers off, or limit how many chunks each network keeps loaded. Then only the chunks nearest the Tether on watch are held, and its panel shows how many of the network's chunks that is. Breaking it A broken Tether keeps its operator inside the item. Its tooltip names it. Recipe

Recipe Cards A Recipe Card holds one recipe for autocrafting. Write it at a Network Encoder, then store it in a Recipe Rack. An empty card has nothing on it. The recipe with an Advanced Logic Chip makes 4. A filled card shows what it makes, and what it takes. A card can hold a crafting recipe, or a processing recipe. A processing card names no machine: pick its recipe in the screen of an Access Port. Cards from older versions that named a port are picked in that port by themselves once their rack has power. A filled card on its own in a crafting grid turns back into an empty one. A card only ever crafts its own recipe. If that recipe is removed or changed (a mod or datapack), the tooltip says Recipe missing and the card doesn't craft. The tooltip tells you which mod the result comes from, whether a card is shaped or shapeless, what goes in, and what comes back. Other items in a slot A card may use another item its recipe takes in a slot (another log for planks), its own item first. A pinned ingredient only ever uses the item on the card. Pin it at the Network Encoder. The tooltip marks it exact. Recipes

Network Chamber Put 8 Network Chambers round a Network Brain, on the same layer, and it becomes a brain floor. Each floor lets the network hold more machines. Towers Stack floors straight on top of each other to make a tower. Every floor needs its own brain in the middle and all 8 of its chambers. A floor with a gap doesn't count, and splits the tower in two. A tower can be 8 floors tall. Floors stacked higher make a tower of their own. A tower shares one pool of power and uses more of it for every floor. Using a tower Cables can join any block of a tower, and a cable on any block powers the whole tower. Right-click any chamber or brain of a tower to open its screen. Chambers don't count toward the machine limit. Recipe One craft makes 4 chambers.

Crafting Decks A Deck with a 3x3 crafting grid. Ingredients come straight from its wafers, and the grid refills itself after every craft. Shift-click the result to craft up to one stack of it into your inventory, or as many as you have materials and room for if that is fewer. When more than one recipe fits the grid, a key above the result opens a row of every result: click one to make it the result. The pick stays until the grid fits something else. With JEI installed, its "+" fills the grid from your wafers and inventory, and fills what it can when something is missing. It also picks JEI's own recipe. Missing ingredients the network can craft show in blue; Ctrl-click asks for them. When you close it, the grid goes back into the wafers. It is also how you ask for autocrafting, and where you set crafting rules. Only Advanced, Elite and Ultimate Decks come in this form. Deck as bucket Right-click a fluid on the Items tab with nothing in hand to pick it, and again to unpick it. A small bucket marks the picked fluid in the grid, and the Deck shows a drop of it in its corner. Sneak + right-click a block to place a bucket of the picked fluid from the Deck's fluid wafers or its network. It follows the vanilla bucket's rules: water fills waterloggable blocks and boils away in the Nether. Sneak + right-click a fluid source to collect a bucket of it. No pick is needed. Getting one Craft a Deck of the same tier, or upgrade from the Crafting Deck below it. Either way it keeps its wafers, its charge and whatever is in its grid. A new Crafting Deck links itself to the network of the Network Encoder you used last. Recipes

Power Most JASM blocks run on FE. Where it comes from Combustion Generators burn fuel. They are the simple answer. Other mods, through the Power Interface. JASM blocks never take power straight from another mod. Batteries store it for later, and charge items in their charging slot. How it travels A generator pushes power into every block it touches. Data Cables carry it through a network, as fast as it comes in. Machines and Archives that touch each other pass power on like a cable. A tower of them needs one cable, or one generator, at any block. Breaking a machine in the middle of a tower cuts off the ones above it, unless a cable reaches them another way. Ports use no power and pass none on to the machines they touch. A port with a Power Upgrade passes power straight on to its machines. What uses it Block Uses Network Encoder 5 FE a tick Recipe Rack 2 FE a tick Crafting Server what its Processors use, only while it has a job Advanced Crafting Server what its Processors use, only while it has a job Network Brain 8 FE a tick alone, 24 with one floor, up to 5,000 with 8 floors Crystal Resonator 10 FE a tick Crystal Foundry 40 FE a tick while it grows Archive 5, 10 or 20 FE a tick by tier Decks and Bitlings have their own batteries. Moving an item through a Deck costs 1 FE.

Storage Modules A job needs room for its ingredients and for everything it makes along the way. That room comes from Storage Modules in the Crafting Server. Module Items of a job 1k 1,000 4k 4,000 16k 16,000 64k 64,000 A server has four module slots, and their room adds up. If a job doesn't fit, the Deck says no server has enough modules. Making one Each size is made from the one below it. 4k needs a Memory Chip, 16k a Link Chip too, and 64k an Advanced Memory Chip. Recipes

Decks A Deck is a handheld reader for your wafers. Put wafers in its side panel and store or take items through the grid, with search, sorting and a few sizes of window. Tier Wafer slots Battery Starter FE Basic FE Advanced FE Elite FE Ultimate FE At a glance (Default values) Power per item moved 1 FE Power Moving an item in or out costs power. Browsing is free. Without charge, a Deck can't move anything. Charge it in a Combustion Generator or anything else that charges items. What a Deck can do Hold item and fluid wafers side by side. See what a Storage Port lends to the network. Right-click a wafer to set its filters and priority. Keep the sorting you picked: every Deck you open sorts the same way. Share its search with JEI's, when JEI is installed. A key on the side turns that off. Network and travel Link to a network at a Network Encoder, to receive port deliveries and see the Network tab. Send items to other players. Work outside the Overworld with a Dimension Upgrade. Opening and wearing Right-click to open the Deck in your hand, or press B (Open Deck, under JASM in Controls) to open the worn Deck, else the first one you carry. With Curios installed, a Deck can be worn in the Deck slot. Every kind of Deck fits. A worn Deck counts as carried: crafting results, port deliveries, rules and sending all find it. If Curios is removed later, a worn Deck comes back to your inventory the next time you join, or drops at your feet when it is full. Upgrading The old Deck is used up. The new one keeps its wafers and its charge. Advanced and above also come as a Crafting Deck. Recipes

Network Encoder The Network Encoder writes recipes onto Recipe Cards. It is also where a Deck gets paired with a network, which unlocks autocrafting, ports and the Network tab. Writing a recipe Click items into the grid. They are only examples and are never used up. Put an empty or filled Recipe Card in. Press Encode. Take the finished card out first, or it can't write the next one. With an empty hand, left-click an ingredient to pin it: a lock shows on the slot, and the card then uses exactly that item, never another one the recipe takes. Click again to unpin. Right-click removes an item from the grid. When more than one recipe fits the grid, the key above the result picks which one the card gets. JEI's "+" picks its own recipe. Two keys beside Encode set the kind of card: the crafting table for Crafting, the furnace for Processing. Crafting is for anything with a crafting grid. JEI's "+" picks the mode by itself: a crafting table recipe switches to Crafting, any other recipe to Processing. Hold Shift on the "+" of a crafting table recipe to write it as a processing card instead, handy for an auto-crafter machine behind an Access Port. For a machine, press Processing and fill the right-hand column with what the machine gives back. The card names no machine: pick the recipe in the screen of the Access Port that should make it. Scroll over a slot to change its amount, or middle-click it and type the amount (fluids in buckets, up to three decimals: 1.25 is 1,250 mB). Right-click with a full bucket or tank to set a fluid. For a machine that only takes some ingredients through its top, bottom or one side, use the Advanced Encoder. The Deck tab shows what is on your Deck. Click an item there for a copy to put in the grid. Nothing leaves the Deck. Pairing a Deck Open the Deck Link window with the side key. Put a Deck in its left slot and take it from the right. Pairing another Deck replaces that player's previous one. Placing the first Network Encoder on a network of your own pairs a Deck you carry, unless it is already paired somewhere. Who may use it The Access window lets the owner trust other players by name, up to 32. Trusted players share recipes but use their own stored items. At a glance Uses 5 FE a tick Counts toward the machine limit Recipe

Training Bitlings A Bitling that works in the Chip Workshop learns from every chip it makes. When its training bar is full, you can grow it up in a crafting grid. The ladder Stage Chips to fill the bar Grows up with Basic Bitling none 8 chips of one type Logic, Memory or Link Bitling 100 7 chips of its type and a Diamond Nibbling 300 7 Advanced chips of its type and a Netherite Scrap Byteling top of the ladder nothing more Put the critter in the middle of the grid and the rest round it. It keeps its charge when it grows up. The real grids are on the pages for Bitlings and Nibblings and Bytelings. Why bother Bigger batteries: 50,000 FE for a Basic Bitling, 150,000 for a typed one, 200,000 for a Nibbling and 400,000 for a Byteling. Better odds of a rare Advanced chip. Only a Byteling can build a Synapse Core.

Befriending Bitlings You find a Basic Bitling in the wild and make friends with it. Where they live Well-lit grass in the Overworld. They turn up now and then. Never in oceans, rivers, beaches, deserts, badlands, mushroom fields, caves or the Deep Dark. They stay where they are, even when you walk away. Growing crystals draw them in. While you are near Seeded Amethyst, a Bitling sometimes wanders over for a look and stays around the crystals for a few minutes. No new one comes once there are about 5 wild Bitlings within 32 blocks. Making friends Hand it a Logic, Memory or Link Chip. An Advanced one works too. It looks the chip over, nods and turns into a Basic Bitling item at its feet. Blank and unquenched chips only get a shake of the head. Hand it a Data Crystal instead and it eats the crystal and follows you for about 30 seconds. It stops if you get more than 24 blocks ahead. Hit one and it runs off. If it is knocked out, it vanishes in a puff and leaves nothing behind. Crafting one On this world you can also craft a Basic Bitling: What next Put your new Basic Bitling to work in the Chip Workshop, or train it into something bigger.

Fluid Type Wafers A few kinds of fluid, each in bulk. Good for water, lava and the other fluids you pump all day. Like a Type Wafer, but for fluids. Wafer Each fluid holds, in buckets Needs 2 fluids 4,096 vanilla items only 4 fluids 16,384 Memory Chip 8 fluids 65,536 Memory Chip 16 fluids 262,144 Link Chip 32 fluids 1,048,576 Advanced Memory Chip 64 fluids 4,194,304 Synapse Core 128 fluids 16,777,216 Synapse Core Every size is made from two wafers of the size before. They are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their fluid and starts unlinked. The 64 and 128 sizes need Synapse Cores. For mixed fluids with no limit on kinds, see Fluid Capacity Wafers. Recipes

Logic and Memory Chips Logic and Memory Chips are the parts most JASM recipes are built from. A Logic Chip comes from an Unquenched Logic Chip: cook a Blank Chip on a Campfire, then drop it in water. A Memory Chip comes from an Unquenched Memory Chip: the same, but in a Blast Furnace. The whole stack cools at once, and no water is used up. Second-tier recipes need them, such as the Basic Deck and the 1K and 4K wafers. The Chip Workshop makes them too. Recipes

Crystal Resonator A powered Crystal Resonator makes the plants and budding blocks next to it grow faster, Seeded Amethyst included. It runs on power from a Data Cable network or a generator next to it. Everything touching it that can grow gets extra growth attempts. It works on Seeded Amethyst, budding blocks, crops, saplings, bamboo, sugar cane, vines, kelp, sweet berries, nether wart and cocoa. Several Resonators add up. Extra growth wears a Seeded Amethyst down less often than natural growth. A seed gives more crystals in total. It doesn't count toward a network's machine limit. At a glance (Default values) Power use 10 FE/t Time between extra growth tries 0.75 seconds Wear chance on Seeded Amethyst 6% Recipe

Capacity Wafers The simple storage chip. A Capacity Wafer holds any mix of items, up to a total. Put it in a Deck or link it to an Archive. Wafer Holds Needs Basic 256 items vanilla items only 1K 1,024 Memory Chip 4K 4,096 Memory Chip 16K 16,384 Memory Chip and Link Chip 64K 65,536 Advanced Memory Chip 256K 262,144 Synapse Core 1M 1,048,576 Synapse Core Upgrading Every size is made from three wafers of the size below. The three are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their items. It starts unlinked, so link it to an Archive again. Fluids have their own wafers: see Fluid Capacity Wafers. For a few item kinds in bulk, use a Type Wafer. Recipes

JASM: Just Another Storage Mod JASM is a digital storage mod built around storing your items and fluids on wafers, upgradeable chips that reside in your personal deck. Connect your Deck to a network of cables and machines, and every item on your wafers can be searched, crafted with and moved from one place. Start here Getting started: the first hour, and what each tier needs. Mechanics: how the systems work. Items, blocks and machines: one page for each, with recipes.

Docking Station A Docking Station holds one Deck for its network, joined by a Data Cable. While the Deck sits in it, ports, crafting jobs, rules and Deck to Deck deliveries use that Deck, whether its owner is online or not. Using it Put in a Deck linked to this network: click or shift-click it into the slot. Only Decks go in. What the docked Deck moves is paid from its own charge, as always. The station charges it from the network's power, so it doubles as a Deck charger. Without charge, the Deck stops until the station fills it again. The station costs nothing to run. It counts toward the machine limit. Deliveries sent to its owner go straight onto its wafers. What doesn't fit waits on its way until there is room. Rules that put their results in your inventory wait until you carry the Deck again. Lock Locked: only the Deck's owner and the network's owner can take it out. A Deck starts locked. Unlocked: anyone trusted on the network can take it out. Only the Deck's owner and the network's owner can lock or unlock it. Breaking the station, or picking it up with a Wrench, follows the same rule. The broken station keeps the Deck inside, locked or not, until it is placed again. Its tooltip says whose Deck it holds. Explosions don't break it. Hoppers, pipes and ports can't take the Deck out. Recipe

Growing Data Crystals Data Crystals are the raw material for everything in JASM. You grow them on a block of amethyst. At a glance (Default values) Wear chance per bud 12% Step by step Craft a Crystal Seed and use it on a Block of Amethyst. It becomes Seeded Amethyst. Buds grow on its open sides, like budding amethyst: small, medium, large, then a full Data Crystal Cluster. Mine the full cluster for Data Crystal, with your hand or any tool. Fortune gives more. A bud broken early gives Crystal Dust instead. Four dust and a redstone make a new seed. The seed wears out Each time a bud grows, the block may wear down one stage: Seeded, Worn, Cracked, then back to a plain Block of Amethyst. Mined at any stage, the block gives the Block of Amethyst back and the seed is lost. Growing faster A powered Crystal Resonator makes a block grow faster. For bulk, the Crystal Foundry turns each Crystal Seed straight into Blank Chips, with no Block of Amethyst to wear out. Visitors Growing crystals draw wild Bitlings. Find out more.

Advanced Encoder A Network Encoder that also picks which face of a machine each ingredient goes in through, and opens the network's Access Ports from afar. For machines that only take some ingredients from the top, the bottom or one side. Leave your machine's own side settings at their defaults, and let the recipe card's faces decide where each ingredient goes. Picking faces Press the furnace key beside Encode for Processing. Open the Faces window with the side key under Deck Link and Access. Click a face key, then click the ingredient slots that go in through it. Right-click or Esc stops. Press Encode as usual. A slot shows its face as a coloured tint with a letter. The faces are Top, Bottom, North, South, East and West, the same whichever way the machine is turned. Default is the face the Access Port touches, as on any card. The Faces window can be dragged anywhere and stays where you left it. Ports The Ports list on the left shows every Access Port on the network you may use, with the machine it works with and its name. The arrow key folds it away. Click a port to open its screen and set it up from here. Closing it brings you back to the encoder. Ports in another dimension are greyed and can't be opened. A port whose machine another port keeps is shown in red. The list needs power, and ports in unloaded chunks aren't shown. Good to know Faces are for ingredients only. Results still come back through the port. A set goes in whole or not at all. If one face says no, nothing goes in through the others. With JEI's "+", ingredients that are the same item get a slot each, so each can have its own face. A machine counts even when the face the port touches takes nothing, as long as another face does. A card's tooltip names the face for each ingredient that doesn't use Default. The Network Encoder shows a card's faces and keeps them when it writes the card again, but can't change them. Recipe
